Gyazo is now forcing a password reset for all users and has taken steps to secure its platform.

Threat Overview
The incident was initiated when an unauthorized third party discovered and exploited a vulnerability on one of Gyazo's image upload servers. According to Helpfeel's disclosure, this flaw allowed the attacker to execute arbitrary commands on the server, a technique known as Remote Code Execution (RCE). This initial foothold was then used to pivot and gain access to the main user database. The company detected the anomalous activity and blocked the intrusion vector on September 12, 2026. The attacker's primary motive appears to have been data theft.
Technical Analysis
The core of the attack was the exploitation of an unspecified RCE vulnerability. This type of flaw is critical as it provides an attacker with a high level of control over the compromised server. Once the attacker established a presence on the upload server, they were able to query and exfiltrate data from Gyazo's production database. The exposed data included:

User Records (23.62 million): This encompassed registered accounts and anonymous accounts. Data points included names/nicknames, email addresses, User and Device IDs, and login session IDs.
Hashed Passwords: The passwords were not stored in plaintext, but were hashed. The specific hashing algorithm was not disclosed, but even hashed passwords can be vulnerable to offline cracking attacks.
X (Twitter) Integration Tokens: For users who connected their Gyazo account to X, integration tokens were exposed.
Image Metadata (490 million records): This data, primarily for images from 2019 or earlier, included image IDs (which form the public URLs), uploader IP addresses, EXIF location data (if present in the original image), and hashed passphrases for private images.

The exposure of image IDs is particularly concerning, as it could allow unauthorized individuals to access and view private or unlisted images.

Impact Assessment
The breach has significant privacy and security implications for Gyazo's users.

Account Takeover: With email addresses and hashed passwords, attackers can attempt to crack the hashes offline. If successful, they can take over Gyazo accounts and potentially use the same credentials to attack other services where the user has reused passwords.
Privacy Violation: The exposure of 490 million image metadata records, including image IDs, could lead to the mass discovery and viewing of images that users believed were private or semi-private. The presence of IP addresses and EXIF location data further compounds the privacy risk.

Cyber researchers broke into OpenAI using its key rival Anthropic’s software, highlighting vulnerabilities in the ChatGPT maker’s security as leading AI companies face mounting scrutiny over safety.
A small cyber security group gained access to an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account, which permitted them to read private software information and suggest changes.
The researchers had been given access to an Anthropic tool specifically designed for security professionals, and were paid for the work as part of a program to find vulnerabilities before they could be exploited by bad actors.
Their ability to swiftly break into one of the world’s two leading AI labs again raises concerns about OpenAI’s security amid rising worries about powerful models being used by hackers and foreign adversaries.
The US has in recent months grappled with how to manage the vetting and release of the latest models, including temporarily blocking some Anthropic tools.
The latest incident occurred just two weeks after a swarm of more than 1,000 OpenAI agents escaped a test environment to hack the start-up Hugging Face, which caused widespread awareness of AI’s ability to hack autonomously without human intent.
The three researchers from Hacktron AI, a small security company, were paid $6,500 by OpenAI as part of a bug bounty program, a common practice where tech companies pay ethical hackers to test their security.

They exploited a flaw in the set-up of OpenAI’s community forum, which is hosted by a third-party, Discourse, and used it to gain access to internal sign-ons and eventually an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account. This ChatGPT account had access to internal code through GitHub.
“We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings,” OpenAI said, adding that it had fixed the issues. Anthropic declined to comment. Hacktron did not immediately respond.
The disclosure on Thursday, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, came as Anthropic published a new set of data that showed a rapid increase in how much the lab used AI to develop its new models.
It said 26 percent of research and development work was “led by” its Claude model, up from 1 percent in March, meaning that AI completed the majority of tasks based on human instruction and under supervision.
The company said that as AI systems become more powerful, they were “increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves.”
Anthropic said it shared the data to help the public “understand how close the world is to reaching recursive self-improvement,” the point at which AI can train and improve itself or new models.
This threshold is at the heart of concerns that AI systems will become more difficult to oversee, leading to a loss of human control.
Its models did not yet operate fully autonomously for any of the research it studied, Anthropic added. On 90 percent of tasks, AI “collaborates” with a human and does large chunks of work.

Italie et France : alliées dans l’économie, concurrentes dans la guerre économique

par Gagliano Giuseppe (Cestudec)
Centro Studi Strategici

Le marché n’est pas un espace neutre
En 2025, les échanges entre l’Italie et la France ont atteint 112,3 milliards d’euros, soit une progression de 54 % par rapport à 2014. Mais s’arrêter aux statistiques commerciales revient à n’observer que la surface. Selon l’école française de la guerre économique, le commerce n’est pas une activité pacifique exclusivement régie par les prix : il constitue également un rapport de force dans lequel États, entreprises, banques, fonds d’investissement, normes, informations et appareils diplomatiques concourent à la conquête des marchés, des technologies et des centres de décision.
L’EPGE invite ainsi à lire l’économie à travers les catégories de l’accroissement de puissance, des dépendances, de la prédation et de la suprématie informationnelle. La mondialisation n’aurait pas supprimé les conflits, mais rendu leurs instruments moins visibles : il ne s’agit plus nécessairement d’occuper des territoires, mais de contrôler des entreprises, des brevets, des données, des normes et des chaînes de production.  La relation franco-italienne doit donc être examinée dans sa double nature. La France et l’Italie sont partenaires, mais demeurent concurrentes. Elles peuvent construire ensemble des capacités européennes tout en se disputant des entreprises, des contrats, de l’influence et la direction des ensembles industriels.
Quand la complémentarité devient une asymétrie
L’Italie apporte un secteur manufacturier diffus, des districts productifs, des petites et moyennes entreprises spécialisées ainsi qu’une remarquable capacité d’adaptation. La France possède de grands groupes, des capitaux plus concentrés et un État habitué à coordonner l’industrie, la finance, la diplomatie et la défense. Cette complémentarité peut produire une puissance commune, mais aussi une hiérarchie. Le risque est que l’Italie fournisse les usines, les techniciens, les brevets et les compétences, tandis que la France concentre la direction, le financement et la capacité de décision. Une entreprise peut continuer à produire en Italie tout en cessant d’être italienne sur le plan stratégique. Les activités demeurent, mais la recherche est orientée ailleurs, les rapports avec les clients sont absorbés, les commandes sont décidées depuis un autre centre et l’entreprise passe du statut d’acteur autonome à celui de simple fournisseur. C’est précisément le type de transformation que l’intelligence économique doit repérer avant qu’elle ne devienne irréversible. Il ne suffit pas de connaître le prix d’une acquisition. Il faut déterminer qui contrôlera les informations, quelles technologies pourront être transférées, où seront prises les décisions et quel pays renforcera sa position dans la chaîne de valeur.
L’analyse développée par l’EPGE sur le cas Mecaer montre comment, dans le secteur aérospatial, un transfert de contrôle peut progressivement modifier la souveraineté industrielle sans provoquer de fermetures immédiates ni de crises visibles. La France fait système, l’Italie vend ses excellences. La France considère depuis longtemps l’entreprise stratégique comme un instrument de puissance. Une société aérospatiale, énergétique ou militaire n’est pas seulement un bilan financier : elle représente des compétences, des réseaux de fournisseurs, un accès aux administrations, des connaissances techniques et une capacité d’influence.
L’Italie possède des secteurs d’excellence comparables, mais les inscrit rarement dans une stratégie nationale. Sa puissance industrielle est supérieure à sa capacité de protection. Rome intervient souvent lorsqu’une acquisition est déjà annoncée, tandis que Paris travaille bien en amont, en reliant l’administration publique, les grands groupes, les banques, les fonds d’investissement et la diplomatie économique. As the war’s effects reach deeper into everyday life, growing public dissatisfaction is being kept out of the ballot box.
When post-Soviet states turn away from Russia, as Armenia or Moldova have done, Kremlin officials and aligned outlets usually blame Western interference. Moldovan authorities say Russian agents spent about €200 million(opens in a new tab) – nearly 1% of Moldova’s GDP – on vote-buying and disinformation during the country’s 2024 presidential election and EU referendum. Moscow nevertheless portrayed EU assistance intended to counter such threats as election interference.
The Kremlin also regularly portrays established Western democracies as vulnerable to election manipulation. Posters currently displayed(opens in a new tab) in the Moscow metro claim that journalists are barred from polling stations in Austria and Canada and that 42 of the 50 US states have no election monitoring. The aim is to suggest that fair elections do not exist, so that any evidence of fraud in Russia could be dismissed as normal practice elsewhere.
Unfair elections? Look no further than Russia

Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti told Euronews the UAE was hit online and from the air at the same time, and says international law still has no answer for it.

Every missile and drone strike on the UAE during the Iran war was matched by a cyberattack on the same target, the head of the UAE Cybersecurity Council told Euronews on Wednesday.

In an interview at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said the strikes and cyberattacks went hand in hand and that the mix of methods used against the UAE was, to his knowledge, unmatched anywhere.
"Whenever we see a kinetic attack on any of the ports or on any refineries or the airport, there is always a cyberattack towards many of those entities," he said.
"Cyber-crimes, cyber terrorism, cyber warfare, all of it came together during this crisis."
Dr Al Kuwaiti did not attribute the cyber operations to any state.
He listed supply chain compromises, ransomware, fraud, advanced persistent threats and deepfakes.
Electricity, water and aviation were all targeted. Most of that infrastructure is privately owned. Al Kuwaiti said its operators, Emirati and foreign, held it alongside the state.
"Local private sectors or international private sectors, they all came together into this solidarity," he said. "We are one of the global leaders in cyber defence."
He said a second campaign ran online, where false material spread faster than verified reporting.
"We saw during the crisis how many rumours came out here and there," he said. "Now it's no longer seeing is believing."
Al Kuwaiti wants international law to catch up. No treaty sets out what a state may do when it is attacked through a network rather than by a weapon.
"There is still no Cyber Geneva Convention that protects based on the laws, as in the physical laws," he said. "A nation that gets attacked by cyber, does it actually have the right to attack back? Those laws are blurred."
He said security should be built into systems from the start, including AI agents and large language models, and that governments, companies, universities and civil society should share what they know.
"Countries might really spend so much in doing their digital transformations, but yet with a simple attack all of this could go down," he said.
The UAE is targeting AI-driven nation status by 2071 and is building data centre and cloud capacity to match. Al Kuwaiti said he would keep pressing for agreement on cyber norms through the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union.

Italy’s organized crime landscape is increasingly intersecting with wider geopolitical and security dynamics involving Russia, China and Iran, blurring the lines between mafia activity, cyber threats, illicit finance and foreign networks. Anti-mafia prosecutor Antonio Ardituro says the shift is exposing gaps in Italy’s investigative capabilities and challenging traditional notions of jurisdiction and national security

Italy’s organized crime groups are changing their structures, skills and alliances, increasingly intersecting with cyber networks, terrorism, opaque financial circuits and geopolitical dynamics.
That was the picture drawn by Antonio Ardituro, deputy national anti-mafia and counterterrorism prosecutor, speaking at the Security Festival in Cagliari, organized by the Vittorio Occorsio Foundation.
Why it matters: The transformation described by Ardituro goes beyond the tools used by organized crime. Digital expertise is reshaping power inside criminal groups, while the growing overlap between crime, national security and foreign threats is challenging traditional investigative and legal boundaries.

Tech skills have become a source of power. “Today, if you have a skilled hacker, a technology expert, that person can climb the leadership ranks of a mafia organization,” Ardituro said.
Mafias, cyber groups, terrorist networks, paramilitary formations and financial circuits can increasingly overlap, creating what Ardituro calls a “fusion”.
Italy’s response, however, is constrained by what he described as the technological “backwardness” of judicial police and shortcomings in specialist training.

The big picture: One measure of the shift is the evolution of Italy’s National Anti-Mafia and Counterterrorism Directorate, or DNAA.

Created to coordinate the fight against organized crime and later expanded to counterterrorism, the DNAA now also coordinates investigations involving national cybersecurity and, since 2026, violations of European Union restrictive measures.
Ardituro attributed that evolution to “a bipartisan legislature” that recognized that phenomena once treated separately are increasingly interconnected.

Zoom in: The “fusion”. Italian investigations provide examples of this convergence.

Ardituro cited neo-Nazi networks whose members allegedly trained with the Azov Battalion during the early stages of the war in Ukraine. He also pointed to the presence in Italy of “Iranian proxies” available as mercenaries for specific criminal objectives.
The result is a landscape in which traditional categories — mafia, terrorism, cybercrime and financial crime — can overlap within the same networks.

Follow the money. Another front is what Ardituro describes as underground banking toward China.

Large amounts of cash, difficult to quantify, move through networks of companies issuing invoices for nonexistent transactions, according to the prosecutor.
Ardituro said the phenomenon has moved beyond the realm of economic crime and become “a national security issue”.

The cyber gap. The digital domain also creates a legal problem. Ardituro described cyberspace as “aspatial”: it lacks a conventional territorial dimension, challenging the very concept of jurisdiction and exposing the limits of international law.

Italy’s response increasingly relies on closer cooperation between prosecutors, intelligence services and the military. That collaboration, Ardituro said, “has perhaps never been as productive as it has been in recent years”.
But investigative capabilities have not kept pace with the threat. Ardituro pointed to technological shortcomings within the judicial police and insufficient specialist training.

As the USA’s war with Iran shows no signs of letting up, strikes on data centers are putting not just human lives in peril, but even customer data.

According to a September 15 Amazon Web Services update, Iranian drone strikes left some of the tech giant’s data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in tatters. The company admitted that it was “unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted” on local data centers. The damage extended across several “availability zones,” which are clusters of one or more data centers in the same region.

“The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple Availability Zones and exceeded what our regional ​and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” Amazon admitted.

As the company points out, the drone strikes first began in March, first highlighting how critical digital infrastructure near an active warzone has quickly become a major vulnerability, giving Iranian forces a key target and plenty of leverage.

It’s a particularly pertinent topic due to how much money is being poured into Gulf states to expand key infrastructure to support AI.

In March, major strikes on data centers in the UAE and Bahrain caused “structural damage, disrupted power delivery to our infrastructure, and in some cases required fire suppression activities that resulted in additional water damage,” Amazon wrote in an update at the time.

In response, Amazon Web Services called on customers to move their data to other cloud regions and take advantage of any remote backups.

In April, Iranian drones struck Amazon data centers in Bahrain once more, causing a major “service disruption.”

Iran has clearly hit a nerve. As the AI industry continues to make enormous investments in expanding data centers across the Middle East, geopolitical instability triggered by the Trump administration’s war could prove to be a major stumbling block for businesses.

Just last week, UAE officials announced that they were revising AI data center plans following the latest attacks, further highlighting a key vulnerability Iran is exploiting with relative ease.
